newsitem.title: GREECE: Hard drachma policy is sustainable - ING Barings.
newsitem.headline: Hard drachma policy is sustainable - ING Barings.

text.p: Greece's hard drachma policy is sustainable despite this week's pressure on the currency ING Barings said, reacting to an Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) report which claimed the opposite.

"Despite this week's turbulence, we feel confident that the Bank of Greece will be able to sustain its hard drachma policy. We forecast a 0-5.0 percent depreciation of the drachma against the ecu this year," ING Barings analyst Yannis Protopapadakis said.

The drachma has depreciated by 0.3 and 0.4 percent versus the ecu and the mark this week. The central bank spent an average $500 million daily during the past four days to defend the currency, he said.
In the year-to-date, the drachma has slid 1.68 percent against the ecu, 0.77 percent against the mark and 10.48 percent against the dollar.
In its 1997-98 outlook on Greece, the EIU said the widening current account deficit was likely to pull the carpet from under the central bank's hard drachma policy and render it unsustainable.

"With a current account deficit which has risen to $4.5 billion or 3.7 percent of GDP in 1996 and which is expected to deteriorate further, the hard drachma policy is unlikely to be sustainable," the EIU said.
It forecast a substantial depreciation of the drachma against core EU currencies in 1998 and against the euro in 1999, assuming that the launch of the single European currency goes ahead on schedule.
Although Greece has a growing current account deficit like the Czech Republic, ING Barings played down concerns that the recent attack against the Czech crown could spread to the drachma.
"We disagree. Greece has more foreign exchange reserves, a lower current account deficit and a longer import cover," Protopapadakis countered.

"Forex reserves were $18 billion in April. If one assumes that $2.0 billion of these have been spent this week defending the drachma, it still leaves us with about 7.5 months of import cover. The current account deficit may be growing in dollar terms, but at 3.9 percent is relatively stable as a percentage of GDP."

In the past the Bank of Greece has fended off speculative attacks with skill. Should reserves prove inadequate, its next most powerful tool will be the country's state-dominated banking sector, he said.
"Seven phone-calls to government appointed bank presidents will give it immediate influence over 86 percent of the country's total deposit base," Protopapadakis said.
Still, falling Greek interest rates have been making the drachma less attractive, posing the question whether this loss of appeal could become a danger.

"Drachma yields are still well above mark and ecu yields. Greek 12-month treasuries yield 9.7 percent, whereas an ecu-based investor would earn 6.7 percent if the drachma fell by 3.0 percent in the next 12 months," Protopapadakis said.

This still compares favourably with the current 3.26 percent yield on mark instruments and the 4.27 percent yield on the ecu -- although it is getting too close to the 6.2 percent yield of U.S. treasuries, he said.
Greece's new 12-month bill coming to market on June 2 will yield a gross 9.6 percent -- 8.9 percent after tax.
